title: Christmas Day
hookLine: many Orthodox keep Christmas on 7 January by the old calendar

cards: Two families, one faith, and two different Christmas mornings. In one house, the feast is today, in December, with the tree and the big meal.

In another, the decorations are still waiting, because their church keeps Christmas in January. Some Orthodox churches still count the year by the older Julian calendar, which has drifted out of step with ours.
Same feast, same story, same child, on a different page of the calendar. And whichever morning it is, the churches gather around one word for what happened.

teach.h: AN OLD WORD FOR A BIRTH.
teach.b: Nativity is an old word for a birth, and the Christian calendar uses it for other births too, but on its own it means this one.
Luke tells it in a single plain sentence: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn."
No description of the baby, no speeches. A manger is an animal's feeding trough: the child's first bed was where the animals ate.

teach.h: UNTO US A CHILD IS BORN.
teach.b: Churches hear another text alongside it, from Isaiah: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder." Read on Christmas, it sounds like a birth announcement.
Christians hear it as fulfilled in Jesus; in Jewish reading, Isaiah is speaking about a king of his own day, and the book was theirs first. Notice the little word us. Not unto the world.
Not unto the righteous. Unto us. Read aloud in church on Christmas morning, it sounds as if whoever is listening is being handed the child.
Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches keep the Nativity, each in its own way.
Orthodox icons show the baby in a dark cave, wrapped so tightly some readers see burial bands, as if the end of the story is folded into the beginning.
Western churches often set up a crib scene, with ox and donkey, shepherds, and later the magi.

teach.h: A CAVE, A CRIB, A FEEDING TROUGH.
teach.b: Underneath every version is the claim Christians build the feast on: that God came near as a newborn, small enough to be laid in a feeding trough.

how: Christians celebrate the Nativity with services on Christmas Eve or Christmas morning, carols, crib scenes and shared meals; some Orthodox churches keep the feast in January because they follow the older Julian calendar.

o: in a borrowed bed in the town.

practice: Let faces come, family, a neighbor, someone working today while others rest, someone spending the day alone, and stay with one person who might not hear a kind word from anyone else.
If you pray, you can hold that person before God with Isaiah's line, unto us a child is born; if you don't, simply hold them in mind with care.

wordCard.voice: Nativity. An old word for a birth, and the Christian name for Christmas: the child wrapped and laid in a manger, because there was no room in the inn.

orig.note: Hebrew: a child — the word in Isaiah's "unto us a child is born" (Isaiah 9:6; 9:5 in Hebrew Bibles).

carryVoice: Your line: unto us a child. The us sounds like whoever is listening. Christmas Day, kept.
